items.title: Essais nucléaires : face au refus français, l’Algérie poursuit seule la décontamination
items.description: Le ministère de la Défense nationale (MDN) annonce le début de la deuxième opération de décontamination d’un site d'essais nucléaires français dans le Sahara algérien. La France refuse toujours de remettre à l’Algérie les registres et cartes de ces essais, rappelle le MDN qui annonce que l’Algérie poursuivra la décontamination avec ses propres moyens et compétences. Essais nucléaires français en Algérie : le MDN lance la deuxième opération de décontamination à In Ekker La date choisie pour rappeler à la France sa responsabilité historique est très symbolique. La deuxième opération de décontamination du site du tunnel d’essais « Béryl 2E », situé dans la région d’In Ekker (Tamanrasset), en 6ᵉ région militaire, a débuté ce dimanche 1ᵉʳ novembre, coïncidant avec la commémoration du 72ᵉ anniversaire du déclenchement de la guerre de Libération nationale. Cette opération, indique le MDN dans un communiqué, entre dans le cadre de la poursuite des opérations de décontamination des anciens sites d’essais nucléaires français dans le Sud du pays et vise à éliminer les déchets radioactifs. Elle est supervisée par le ministère de la Défense nationale, en coordination avec l’Agence nationale de réhabilitation des anciens sites d’essais et d’explosions nucléaires français dans le Sud de l’Algérie, « conformément aux normes nationales et internationales en vigueur », ajoute la même source. Refus de la France de fournir les cartes des sites des essais nucléaires L’opération est menée grâce « aux compétences et aux moyens nationaux », précise le MDN, qui réitère que la France persiste dans son refus de remettre à l’Algérie les données (registres et cartes) de ces essais. Face à ce refus, l’Algérie poursuivra les opérations avec ses propres moyens et compétences jusqu'à la décontamination totale. « Devant le refus par la partie française d’assumer ses responsabilités pénales et de fournir les documents et cartographies des sites d’enfouissement de ces déchets nucléaires, qui constituent encore un handicap pour le développement des régions d’In Ekker à Tamanrasset et de Reggane à Adrar, les compétences nationales sont déterminées à œuvrer pour l’assainissement total des déchets nucléaires hérités du colonisateur français dans notre grand Sud et assurer leur réhabilitation à l’avenir », a indiqué le MDN dans le communiqué. « Un véritable défi pour les compétences nationales » Toutes les ressources matérielles et humaines ont été mobilisées par l’État algérien pour cette « opération complexe », assure le MDN. Ce qui, poursuit la même source, représente « un véritable défi pour les compétences nationales qui veilleront à la réussite de cette mission, dans le strict respect de toutes les conditions de sécurité, des protocoles et des normes internationales relatives à la délimitation des zones radioactives, au ramassage des déchets nucléaires et à leur stockage dans des conteneurs en béton prévus à cet effet ». La France a mené, entre 1960 et 1967, 17 essais nucléaires, 13 souterrains et 4 atmosphériques, à Reggane et In Ekker, dans le Sahara algérien. Plus de 65 ans après, ces sites sont toujours contaminés et les déchets radioactifs constituent une source de danger pour les habitants. L’article Essais nucléaires : face au refus français, l’Algérie poursuit seule la décontamination est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Mutuelle des membres du BBDA : C’est acté pour Teel-taaba BBDA !
items.description: C’est désormais officiel : la mutuelle sociale des membres du Bureau Burkinabè du Droit d’Auteur (BBDA) s’appelle « Teel taaba BBDA ». Ce nom a été consacré le samedi 31 octobre 2026, lors de l’Assemblée générale constitutive tenue dans la salle de conférence du Liptako-Gourma, à Ouagadougou. Portée par le BBDA avec le soutien du ministère de la Communication, de la Culture, des Arts et du Tourisme, cette initiative vise à renforcer la protection sociale des créateurs et des autres acteurs culturels membres, notamment en matière de prise en charge sanitaire. Elle s’inscrit dans la dynamique de promotion de la protection sociale des acteurs culturels, chère au ministre, le Camarade Pingdwendé Gilbert OUÉDRAOGO. Après le discours d’ouverture du Directeur Général du BBDA, le Camarade Zita Daniel BONZI, les participants ont suivi la présentation des statuts et du règlement intérieur. Les échanges, francs et constructifs, conduits par le bureau de séance présidé par le doyen Gustave SORGHO, ont permis d’enrichir les textes et de poser les bases d’une gouvernance participative et responsable. Au terme des travaux, les membres ont unanimement adhéré à la mise en place de la mutuelle, adopté ses textes fondamentaux et élu un Conseil d’administration de vingt (20) membres. Cet organe veillera à la bonne administration de la mutuelle, à la préservation de ses ressources et à la mise en œuvre de ses missions au bénéfice des adhérents. À l’issue de l’assemblée, le Directeur Général a exprimé sa satisfaction. Il a rappelé que le BBDA avait été créé dans un contexte révolutionnaire et que, plus de quarante ans après, la mutuelle de ses membres voit le jour dans ce même contexte. « Je souhaite que cette mutuelle aille très loin. C’est une chance historique que nous avons : profitons de cela », a-t-il déclaré, en invitant les membres à s’approprier cet instrument de solidarité et à œuvrer à sa pérennisation. Sa réussite dépendra désormais de l’engagement de ses membres, de leur adhésion effective, de la régularité de leurs cotisations et de la rigueur de sa gestion. Car protéger les créateurs, c’est aussi préserver celles et ceux qui font vivre la culture burkinabè. BBDA : gérer efficacement les droits protégés, promouvoir les talents, bâtir l’avenir culturel ! items.title: Adeleke, Oyetola unite to deliver 1.5m votes for Tinubu
items.description: Tompolo donates 30 campaign vehicles, launches 10,000 canvassers By Shina Abubakar, Osogbo The re-election campaign of President Bola Tinubu in Osun State received a boost at the weekend as Governor Ademola Adeleke and his predecessor, Adegboyega Oyetola, pledged to work together to secure victory for the President in the 2027 election. The commitment came as the Grand Patron of the President Bola Tinubu Door-to-Door Movement, High Chief Government Ekpemupolo, popularly known as Tompolo, launched 10,000 canvassers and donated 30 campaign vehicles and public address systems to support the mobilisation drive. Speaking at the launch held at Freedom Park, Osogbo, representatives of Adeleke and Oyetola called on political leaders and stakeholders to set aside their differences and work towards delivering the targeted 1.5 million votes for Tinubu in the state. Oyetola, Minister of Marine and Blue Economy, who was represented by Bola Oyebamiji, urged the canvassers to approach the assignment with sincerity, discipline and commitment. He cautioned them against hypocrisy, political pretence and complacency, while appealing to political leaders, interest groups and other stakeholders to put aside personal interests and differences. “I appeal to all political leaders, interest groups, individuals and stakeholders to rise above selfish interests, personal ego and political differences. Let us demonstrate that political differences need not prevent us from pursuing a shared national objective. “With unity of purpose, effective grassroots mobilisation and unwavering commitment, we can deliver the 1.5 million votes targeted for President Bola Ahmed Tinubu in Osun State and secure victory for our party’s candidates at all levels,” he said. In his remarks, Adeleke, who is the state coordinator of the Presidential Campaign Council and was represented by his deputy, Kola Adewusi, described the launch of the canvassers and donation of vehicles as timely for the commencement of the President’s campaign in the state. He urged coalition partners to put aside past disagreements and work together, saying the partnership was focused primarily on the presidential election. “Our gathering is therefore a timely push to gain further momentum in the campaign process. We must therefore forget past disagreements and unite to deliver for the President. “All coalition partners have a duty to overlook all previous relationship antagonism and join hands to deliver between 1.5 to 2 million votes for Mr President,” he said. Earlier, Tompolo, who was represented by the Managing Director of Tantita Security Services Nigeria Limited, Dr Kestin Pondi, said the movement was targeting at least 90 per cent of the votes in Osun for Tinubu. “We know that you are already going to vote for your brother. We know that you are already going to vote for your son. We know that you are already going to vote for the man who is moving Nigeria forward. But what we are going to tell you is that we don’t want your vote to be less than 90%,” he said. Also speaking, the APC National Secretary, Dr Ajibola Basiru, said the canvassers would take the campaign to communities across the state to educate residents on the policies and programmes of the Tinubu administration. He cited the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND) and ongoing road projects as reasons for supporting the President’s re-election. Basiru listed the Ilesa-Ife-Ibadan Expressway, Osogbo-Gbongan Expressway and Osogbo-Iwo-Ibadan roads among the infrastructure projects, adding that the canvassers would explain the administration’s policies to residents. The Osun State Coordinator of the PBAT Door-to-Door Movement, Adeolu Timothy, pledged that the canvassers would deliver on their mandate through effective grassroots mobilisation and monitoring. He said the movement would reach residents across the state and encourage them not only to vote for Tinubu but also to support the campaign at the grassroots. items.title: Minimum Wage: NLC sets agenda for next negotiations
items.description: *Decries poor pay, job insecurity, no welfare protection for Nigerian journalists By Victor Ahiuma-Young & Omotola Aremo The Nigeria Labour Congress, NLC, has identified inflation, the cost of living, the value of the naira, transportation, housing and workers’ purchasing power as major issues that must shape the next national minimum wage negotiations. While insisting that discussions should commence far before April 2027 implementation, the Congress also expressed concern over the poor welfare conditions of Nigerian journalists. The NLC lamented that Nigerian journalists are faced daunting harsh working conditions including inadequate salaries, job insecurity, weak pension arrangements and the absence of effective social security protection, calling on the Nigeria Union of Journalists (NUJ) to take its trade union responsibilities more seriously. The NLC President of NLC, Joe Ajaero, spoke weekend in Lagos, at the 2026 Labour Writers Association of Nigeria, LAWAN, Annual Conference in Lagos, themed; “Workers at the centre of Nigeria’s Political Transition: Defending rights, advancing welfare and building economic justice”. He contended that the next minimum wage must reflect prevailing economic realities rather than arbitrary figures that could quickly lose their value to inflation. Speaking on workers’ welfare and collective bargaining, the NLC President said: “We must examine inflation, the value of the naira and other factors affecting workers’ purchasing power. The new minimum wage should be informed by the cost-of-living index and prevailing inflationary trends.” He maintained that negotiations must take into consideration the cost of accommodation, transportation, food and other basic necessities before an acceptable wage is determined. According to him, it would be counterproductive to negotiate a new minimum wage without establishing what the proposed amount could actually purchase. He warned that workers should not find themselves receiving an improved salary only for inflation to erode its value within a few months, forcing them to demand another increase. According to him: “We must not approach the next minimum wage negotiation by simply demanding millions or billions without considering other economic factors. “We must consider inflation, the value of the currency and other issues affecting the economy. The new minimum wage should be determined with reference to the cost-of-living index and inflationary trends. “If the government agrees that wages should be indexed to inflation, then an increase in inflation should lead to an appropriate adjustment in wages. “Alternatively, we must examine the prices of essential commodities and services. How much does a bag of garri cost? How much is house rent? How much does transportation cost? These are the factors that must inform the negotiations. “We cannot simply announce that we want ₦100,000 or ₦50,000 without establishing how those figures relate to the actual cost of living. This is important because, over the years, we have repeatedly found ourselves in a situation where workers receive a salary increase, but within a few months, inflation erodes its value and they are already demanding another adjustment. We must avoid that situation. “The government must take a more decisive position on solving the transportation problem. Giving workers ₦70,000 as a transportation intervention for six months is not enough, although it provides some relief. For somebody earning ₦70,000, receiving another ₦70,000 is certainly meaningful. “But what happens after six months?There are also other policies that must be considered, particularly transportation. We cannot accept a situation where workers receive ₦70,000 as temporary relief and, after six months, the government simply withdraws the intervention without providing an alternative. “Nobody should assume that because the six-month period has expired, workers must return to their previous state of poverty. We have left Egypt; we cannot go back to Egypt. “As far as the minimum wage negotiations are concerned, the new negotiations must recognise the existing wage structure and the improvements already achieved. You cannot begin negotiating from a position that ignores those gains. “You cannot expect workers to return to the old minimum wage position of ₦70,000 after receiving the additional intervention. We must consolidate the gains already made. Journalists welfare On the welfare of journalists, the NLC challenged the NUJ to intensify its involvement in collective bargaining and negotiations with media employers to secure better conditions of service for its members. The labour leader questioned the absence of effective collective bargaining agreements in the media industry, asking: “What is the minimum wage for media workers across the country? What collective bargaining agreements exist between journalists and their employers?” He argued that journalism being a professional occupation does not remove the need for trade union representation, noting that the NUJ is already registered as a trade union and should actively negotiate improved salaries and welfare packages. He observed that most journalists depend on employment in media organisations for their livelihoods, unlike some professionals who can establish private businesses or independent practices. “Therefore, the NUJ must be actively involved in negotiating better welfare packages for its members,” he said. Ajaero also called for the revival of the proposed journalists’ village initiative and partnerships between journalists and mortgage institutions to enable media workers to own houses through affordable payment arrangements. On job security and retirement benefits, the labour leader lamented that many journalists frequently move from one media organisation to another because of poor remuneration and unfavourable conditions of service. He noted that low salaries also translate into inadequate pension contributions, leaving many workers financially vulnerable after retirement. The NLC President called for improved salaries, stronger employment protection, better pension arrangements and comprehensive social security provisions for journalists. items.title: Ligue1: Achraf Hakimi "plus qu’un simple défenseur"
items.description: L’international marocain Achraf Hakimi a démontré, lors du match opposant vendredi dernier Paris Saint-Germain (PSG) au Havre dans le cadre de la 9e journée de Ligue 1, qu’il peut être bien « plus qu’un simple défenseur », souligne dimanche le journal tunisien « Le Quotidien ». Avec un triplé et ses deux passes décisives, « l’international marocain confirme une nouvelle fois son importance dans le dispositif parisien et démontre qu’il peut être bien plus qu’un simple défenseur », écrit le journal. Le latéral marocain, qui a livré une performance « de très haut niveau », contribuant à la large victoire parisienne (5-1), a confirmé son « aisance dans les phases offensives », commente le média dans son article intitulé « Achraf Hakimi illumine le PSG avec un triplé et deux passes décisives ». Qualifiant la prestation du joueur marocain (27 ans) d’ »exceptionnelle » face au Havre, le journal précise qu’il a « pris les choses en main » et a participé à l’intégralité des réalisations de son équipe, faisant encore parler « sa qualité technique » et signant ainsi une première dans sa carrière. À l’issue de cette rencontre, Hakimi n’a pas caché sa satisfaction, fait savoir la publication, relevant que « malgré son statut de latéral droit de formation, il apprécie particulièrement la liberté offensive que lui accorde son entraîneur Luis Enrique ». Il s’agit d’une « liberté qui lui permet de multiplier les appels et de se retrouver régulièrement dans les zones de finition », ajoute « Le Quotidien ». items.title: Prince Adu-Owusu: Your person will find you
items.description: There is something I want you to remember, especially if you have been through a heartbreak that has made you question whether you will ever experience love the way you once imagined it: your person will find you eventually. I know that may sound like something people say to make a hurting heart feel better. I know that when you are struggling to move on from someone you genuinely loved, hearing that there is someone else out there for you may not immediately change how you feel. You may have heard it from friends, family and people who genuinely want to see you happy. Yet, when the day ends and you are alone with your thoughts, the pain is still there. You still miss someone. You still wish things had turned out differently, and somewhere inside you, there is still a little hope that perhaps things could work out again. Sometimes, the hardest part of heartbreak is having to see the person you once imagined a future with continue living their life with someone else while you are still trying to understand how yours changed so suddenly. Although you try to act as though everything is fine, but something inside you shifts. You become uncomfortable.You begin to question whether they have found in someone else what they once had with you, and whether the memories you still hold so dearly mean anything to them anymore. You may want to ask questions, but you know that some answers will only make the situation more difficult. So you keep quiet, put on a brave face and try to carry on with your day. There are moments when the pain becomes so overwhelming that you struggle to concentrate on anything else. You replay conversations, revisit memories and wonder what you could have done differently. You may even begin to question your own worth, as though someone’s decision not to continue with you is a reflection of everything you are or are not. But it is not. A relationship ending does not mean your life has ended. It does not mean your dreams must be put on hold, your ambitions must disappear or your happiness must depend on whether someone chooses to return. It does not mean that because one person could not give you the future you wanted, nobody else will ever be willing to build that future with you. And perhaps this is where we need to remind ourselves that life is not a competition or a timeline in which everyone must find love, get married or settle down at a particular age. You are not behind because a relationship ended. You are not less deserving of love because someone you wanted did not choose to stay. You have not exhausted your chances of finding happiness simply because one chapter of your life did not end the way you hoped. Sometimes, we become so attached to the person we have lost that we forget there is still a whole life waiting for us beyond that relationship. We forget the things we wanted to achieve before we met them. We forget the ambitions we carried, the places we wanted to visit, the experiences we wanted to have and the person we were becoming before the relationship became such a significant part of our lives. You can find someone who makes you laugh in ways you never expected. Someone who enjoys your company, listens to your concerns, celebrates your achievements and takes an interest in the little details of your life. Someone who makes you feel wanted without making you question your place in their world. Someone who does not simply talk about a future with you but is intentional about building one. And that word matters: intentionality. I think one of the most beautiful things about being loved is knowing that someone is intentional about having you in their life. It is not just the sweet messages, romantic gestures, gifts or promises. It is the consistency behind them. It is someone who checks on you because they genuinely want to know how you are doing. Someone who makes time for you even when life gets busy. Someone who does not leave you constantly guessing where you stand. Someone who understands that love requires effort, consideration, honesty and responsibility. It is the comfort of knowing that you are not the only person trying to make the relationship work. You are not always the one initiating conversations, planning moments together, apologising or finding ways to keep the connection alive. The effort is mutual. The affection is mutual. The desire to build something meaningful is mutual. That is the kind of love I hope everyone gets to experience. Because saying you love someone is one thing; making that person feel loved through your actions is another. You can tell someone they mean the world to you, but if your actions constantly make them feel unwanted, uncertain or unimportant, eventually those words begin to lose their meaning. Love should not be a guessing game in which one person is always trying to interpret the other person’s intentions. Your person will not necessarily be someone who never makes mistakes or disappoints you. No relationship comes without its challenges. But it should be someone who is willing to communicate, take responsibility, make adjustments and work through difficult moments with you. Someone who understands that keeping a person in your life requires more than making promises when everything is going well. That is why I want you to remain hopeful. Do not allow the pain of a relationship that did not work to convince you that love itself has failed you. Do not allow the experience of being left, misunderstood, or taken for granted to make you believe that you must settle for whatever affection comes your way. You deserve a relationship in which you do not have to keep begging for the very things that make love meaningful. I understand that letting go is not always as simple as people make it sound. You can know that a relationship has ended and still have feelings for the person. You can wish them well and still feel uncomfortable seeing them with someone else. You can be making progress in your healing and still have days when the memories return with a force you did not expect. Healing does not mean you suddenly stop caring. It means you gradually learn not to let those feelings determine the direction of your life. You may have tried to make things work. You may have reached out, had difficult conversations, apologised, made compromises and given the relationship more chances than you ever imagined you would. And perhaps, despite all those efforts, things still did not work out. At some point, you must understand that a relationship cannot be sustained by the determination of one person alone. Two people must want to build it. There are still conversations you have not had, places you have not visited, memories you have not created and people you have not met. Somewhere along the way, you may meet someone whose presence will remind you that love does not always have to feel like uncertainty. Someone who will appreciate the things you once felt were too much to ask for. Someone who will not make you feel guilty for wanting attention, affection, reassurance and consistency. And when that happens, I hope you recognise the difference between someone who simply wants to enjoy your presence and someone who is genuinely intentional about keeping you in their life. Until then, live. Continue pursuing your dreams. Take care of yourself. Reconnect with the things that make you happy. Spend time with people who remind you that you are loved beyond romantic relationships. Give yourself the opportunity to grow into the person you want to become. Do not make your happiness wait for someone else to arrive. I cannot promise you when your person will find you, what they will look like or where your paths will cross. But I believe that one relationship ending should never be enough reason to give up on the possibility of experiencing a beautiful one again. Dear reader, if you are still trying to recover from someone you once loved, I hope you hold on to this thought: you have not missed your only opportunity to be loved. You have not reached the end of your story. And you do not have to spend the rest of your life looking back at someone who could not continue the journey with you. Your person will find you eventually. And when love comes again, may it be accompanied by the kind of intentionality that makes you feel secure, appreciated and genuinely wanted. Because the end of one love story does not mean you have run out of love. Sometimes, it simply means there are still chapters ahead that you have not yet had the chance to read. ********** The writer is an online journalist and a freelance graphic designer with The Multimedia Group. items.title: The Menacing MAGA Way to Remake European Politics
items.description: At a dinner in Athens in March, Kimberly Guilfoyle, then the U.S. ambassador to Greece, made a statement that elegantly combined arrogance with menace. According to The Wall Street Journal and the Financial Times , Guilfoyle referred to the troubles of Romania’s governing coalition and, with Greek politicians in the room, took credit for its impending collapse: “We can do that to any country we want,” she said. “We can do that here.” Guilfoyle was subsequently disgraced for a different reason: The Journal also obtained screenshots of messages she had sent to a Republican donor, asking him to deposit $100,000 in her American Express account. She and her lawyer denied everything, including the dinner conversation, but the screenshots were too much even for the Trump administration. She resigned. If Americans were more exercised by her apparent greed, Europeans were appalled by her political boasts. Guilfoyle did seem to think she could influence the coalition politics of democratically elected European governments, all of them U.S. allies and members of NATO. More to the point, she isn’t the only Trump-administration official who has tried to do exactly that. Americans once promoted democracy in Europe as a political system, and under that general understanding accepted all elected politicians of the center-left and center-right as legitimate. This administration and its adjacent business elite are now pursuing a different policy. In some cases, they promote the interests of parties that they believe to be ideologically aligned with the MAGA movement, including some that are openly pro-Russian. Other European political figures seem to have gained Washington’s blessing (or are trying to gain it) because they can promote commercial interests favored by someone close to the administration. In at least three cases, Americans have reportedly tried to persuade elected European leaders to dump their current coalition partners in favor of new ones more to the White House’s liking. [ Tom Nichols: Kimberly Guilfoyle broke Trump’s most important rule ] The clearest case is in Poland. I am married to Polish Foreign Minister Radek Sikorski, whose political party is the largest member of the current ruling coalition. But I am not revealing any special information; Polish media, including far-right media, have widely reported that President Trump strongly hinted to the leader of one of the coalition’s two other parties that he should switch sides. The politician in question is Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, the leader of the small, agrarian Polish People’s Party. He was in Washington, D.C., in the spring to attend a Medal of Honor ceremony for an American soldier who had saved the life of a Polish soldier in Afghanistan. Just after the event, which was organized by Polish activists with MAGA contacts, Kosiniak-Kamysz was taken aside by the president, who reportedly told him that he would be much better regarded in Washington if he left the government coalition: He should do a deal with Polish-nationalist and far-right parties instead. He didn’t follow Trump’s advice. ( The Atlantic requested comment about the incident from the White House but has not yet received a response.) This was not the first time the Trump administration had made its sympathies in Poland clear. During the Polish presidential-election campaign last year, the far-right candidate Karol Nawrocki visited Washington, where Trump endorsed his bid. After Nawrocki won, Trump repeatedly took credit for the victory, just as he and his entourage have taken credit for electoral victories in Latin America. Nevertheless, this latest story feels different. An American president asking a politician in an allied foreign country to change coalitions? Nothing like it has happened in Poland since the days when Soviet leaders decided which Polish Communists should rule. Guilfoyle doesn’t have Trump’s power, but as his ambassador, she seemed unusually versed in the internal details of Romanian politics, even though she was posted to Athens. At the end of March, she appeared on a panel at a business conference in Bucharest and spoke about the “vertical gas corridor,” a pipeline system linking Greece, Romania, Ukraine, and other countries in southeastern Europe. Although she had no previous background in gas infrastructure, she became an enthusiast during her stay at the U.S. embassy in Greece. Indeed, Christos Marafatsos, a lobbyist for Aktor Group, a Greek company with interests in the pipeline system, frequently traveled with Guilfoyle, so much so, according to the Journal , that “some foreign officials mistook him for her chief of staff.” The CEO of Aktor was also at the Bucharest event, speaking just after Guilfoyle. And during her event, Guilfoyle advocated for not just the construction of the infrastructure, but also the purchase of American liquefied natural gas; Aktor has an interest in both matters. Ilie Bolojan, the Romanian prime minister at the time, was a supporter of the pipeline project, he recently confirmed. But he was not interested in locking Romania into a gas-purchase contract, both because the price was not competitive and because Romania is gearing up to export its own gas. Others were. On the same trip, Guilfoyle was also seen (and filmed) having dinner at an expensive restaurant in Bucharest with one of Bolojan’s coalition partners, Sorin Grindeanu, the leader of the Romanian Social Democratic Party, and several other Romanian politicians. One of those present, a former energy minister, was interested in buying American LNG and reportedly wrote to the prime minister and the president, calling for exactly that. Over the next couple of months, Grindeanu’s Social Democrats would leave the ruling coalition and then join the Romanian far-right party in supporting a vote of no confidence in Bolojan’s liberal-centrist government, forcing him to resign. Grindeanu has denied emphatically that Guilfoyle or any other American influenced his decision. The leader of the Romanian far right, George Simion, a pro-Russian politician who has sought to build relations with MAGA influencers close to Trump, described himself as a “good friend” of Guilfoyle but also denied that she had affected the decision. Still, it’s not hard to see why some Romanians think she did. One notable feature of the Romanian government’s collapse was its orchestration by two political parties, one ostensibly on the center-left, the other of the far right. By working together, they broke a so-called firewall, a long-standing determination to exclude political parties and leaders sympathetic to fascism from mainstream politics. The same firewall exists in Germany, where the conservative Christian Democratic Union runs the government with the center-left Social Democrats as a junior partner. Some German politicians believe that the Trump administration wants the CDU to break the firewall and form a coalition with the far-right AfD (Alternative for Germany) instead. AfD is openly pro-Russian, and some of its politicians have had neo-Nazi affiliations. For many Christian Democrats, members of a conservative party founded in the postwar era as a bulwark against extremism, joining with AfD is an almost unimaginable break with their values. [ Anne Applebaum: MAGA is making the world safe for corruption ] Rather than approaching CDU leaders directly, Trump has used his Truth Social account to promote AfD, publicly cheering the party’s victory in recent regional elections: “THEY ARE ON THE RISE,” he wrote, “and not going to take it anymore!” Elon Musk, the administration’s close ally and the Republican Party’s most significant donor, virtually attended an AfD event before the most recent Bundestag election. Because Musk’s X algorithm gives enormous weight to posts from his account, this amounted to a large, free promotion for AfD. Several German politicians mentioned another incident, on which I have previously reported . Earlier this year, a group of legislators from various political parties came to Washington and arranged meetings at the Pentagon and State Department. According to a senior member of the CDU, they were told that only representatives from AfD and the CDU could enter the buildings; members of the Social Democratic Party, who are part of the government coalition, were not allowed. Neither were others. The CDU members declined to go at all. The party leadership understood the gesture as a message to them: The only partner we recognize is AfD . This gesture demonstrated what is probably the Trump administration’s authentic contempt for German democracy. But it also revealed a deep contradiction in U.S. foreign policy. On the one hand, American officials encourage Europeans to build up their own military forces. Speaking at NATO headquarters last summer, Elbridge Colby, an undersecretary of defense, said that in the future, American allies should be “taking primary responsibility for Europe's conventional defense.” Germany, Poland, and Romania are all countries that have taken this request seriously. But on the other hand, the same administration is directly promoting the fortunes of political parties and leaders who oppose defense spending, who favor Russia, or who do not promise to defend Europe or respect European borders. Alice Weidel, AfD’s co-leader, opposes offering military aid to Ukraine and also argues against defense cooperation with other European countries. The party’s co-chair Tino Chrupalla has called for the expulsion of American troops from Germany. George Simion, the leader of the Romanian far right, has in the past advocated for the restoration of Romania’s pre-1940 borders, including territory now in Ukraine. The Polish far right has lately begun repeating anti-European and anti-Ukrainian narratives of a kind that are now popular in both Washington and Moscow, undermining support for a unified European defense. In effect, the administration is promoting European rearmament and European defense cooperation while simultaneously promoting politicians who oppose rearmament or defense cooperation. Across democratic Europe, the public and the politicians are confused. Once, Europeans generally believed that America promoted democracy—the political system, not particular parties—and staunchly opposed Russia and other authoritarian regimes. Now, it seems, Trump-administration officials have flipped the script. Some of them, like Guilfoyle, seem more interested in commercial deals than in security. Others seem to be pursuing dangerous goals. Does America want Europeans to build large armies—and then to break up European institutions and hand those armies over to nationalists? That policy was tried in the 20th century. It failed quite dramatically.

items.title: Je suis volontaire donc je suis ! ( par Arame NDIAYE)
items.description: Il y a des badges qui ouvrent des portes. Et puis, il y a ceux qui semblent ouvrir les portes de l’ego ! À l’occasion des Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse (JOJ) Dakar 2026, prévus du 31 octobre au 13 novembre, une petite guéguerre se joue sur les réseaux sociaux, notamment sur TikTok. Au menu : rivalités, petites piques et démonstrations de statut. C’est bien connu, au Sénégal, on aime les choses qui se voient. Dans un pays du m’as-tu-vu, du paraître et du blingbling, le fait d’être volontaire pour les JOJ est devenu la nouvelle tendance à afficher sur les réseaux sociaux. De l’unboxing (l’action d’ouvrir l’emballage d’un produit neuf pour la première fois devant une caméra ou en direct), en passant par les équipements, rien n’est laissé au hasard pour flâner, frimer, narguer ceux qui n’ont pas su saisir la perche. Certes, être volontaire pour un événement d’une telle envergure est une belle expérience. C’est l’occasion de découvrir les coulisses d’une organisation internationale, d’acquérir des compétences, de rencontrer du monde, de réseauter et de participer à un moment historique pour le Sénégal. Il y a de quoi être fier. Mais depuis quand la fierté nécessite-t-elle de regarder les autres de haut ? Sur TikTok, le badge peut vite devenir un accessoire de prestige. La tenue officielle, une preuve d’appartenance à un cercle privilégié. L’accès aux coulisses, un argument pour rappeler aux autres qu’on fait partie des élus. Et ceux qui n’ont pas été sélectionnés ? Ils n’ont qu’à regarder les vidéos et apprécier le spectacle ! Du moins, c’est l’impression que peut donner cette rivalité lorsqu’elle s’installe. Le phénomène n’est pourtant pas nouveau. Dans notre société, l’accès à certaines opportunités peut rapidement devenir un marqueur social. Avoir décroché un stage dans une institution prestigieuse, participer à un programme international ou être invité à un événement sélectif donne parfois l’impression d’avoir franchi un palier que les autres n’ont pas atteint. Sur les réseaux sociaux, où chaque expérience peut devenir une vitrine, la tentation de transformer une opportunité en trophée est encore plus forte. Le problème, ce n’est donc pas de montrer sa joie, de publier ses photos ou de raconter son expérience. Les réseaux sociaux sont aussi faits pour ça. Le problème commence lorsque le partage se transforme en démonstration, et que la démonstration sert à rabaisser ceux qui n’ont pas eu la même chance. Car oui, une sélection reste une sélection. Elle répond à des critères, à un nombre de places disponibles et à des besoins précis. Elle ne constitue pas un classement général de la valeur humaine ! Et c’est là que le paradoxe devient intéressant. Le volontariat est censé incarner la solidarité, le dévouement et l’esprit d’équipe. On s’engage pour contribuer à une œuvre collective, pas pour décrocher un titre de noblesse. Si le badge devient un permis de mépriser les autres, il y a peut-être un petit problème de compréhension de la mission. Parce qu’au fond, être volontaire, c’est être au service d’un événement. Ce n’est pas devenir l’événement lui-même. Et si l’on veut vraiment jouer dans la cour des grands, commençons peut-être par une petite leçon d’humilité. Celle-là, malheureusement, ne figure dans aucun kit officiel ! Arame NDIAYE

items.title: PIA's first Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner arrives in Islamabad
items.description: Pakistan International Airlines’ (PIA) first Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner, acquired on lease last month, arrived in Islamabad from London as flight PK786 on Sunday. A PIA spokesperson, in a statement, said that the carrier is the first Pakistani airline to have added a Boeing 787-9 to its fleet. PIA Chief Executive Aamir Hayat, accompanied by his team, welcomed the Dreamliner at Islamabad airport, according to the statement. The plane is equipped with modern technology, including in-flight entertainment, and features a spacious and comfortable cabin, PIA said. “The inclusion of the Dreamliner is part of a strategy to modernise PIA’s fleet and strengthen its international network,” the spokesperson said. Photo shows the inside of the Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner, which arrived in Islamabad on Sunday. — Photo courtesy PIA “PIA’s objective is to provide international-standard travel facilities and a more comfortable air travel experience to passengers through modern aircraft.” The Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner is a long-range, twin-engine plane with up to 325 seats. Previously, PIA’s fleet consisted of 12 Boeing 777 jets, 15 Airbus A320 planes and five smaller ATRs. Photo shows the inside of the Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner, which arrived in Islamabad on Sunday. — Photo courtesy PIA Last month, PIA signed an ACMI (aircraft, crew, maintenance, and insurance) lease agreement with Norse Atlantic Airways to acquire two state-of-the-art Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners, one of which arrived in Islamabad on Sunday. A PIA spokesperson at the time said the addition of the Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner would mark the start of the airline’s expansion. By expanding its fleet, the airline aims to meet rising demand with direct flights and broader global connectivity, he added. The aircraft would operate direct long-haul flights from Pakistan to the United Kingdom, he said, adding that they would support PIA operations between different points in the UK and Pakistan. The development also comes as the government in September clarified that it was not buying any aircraft for the former national carrier after reports emerged of a federal minister arranging and negotiating sovereign-linked financing for PIA jets. PIA was privatised in December last year through an auction. A consortium led by Arif Habib Corporation Limited had won the auction for 75 per cent shares of PIA in December last year, making a winning bid of Rs135 billion. The Arif Habib-led consortium had vowed to transform the loss-making airline through operational restructuring, fleet expansion, and improved customer service.

items.title: Pakistan’s past and future make a bid for the present
items.description: Whatever there is to be said about Fakhar Zaman has been said. And he has usually said it himself – first when he made his debut and steered Pakistan to their greatest triumph of the past decade, then countless times for Lahore Qalandars, then on that one rainy day in Bangalore, climbing a mountain no one had given him a shot at. Fakhar has had a long few years, with recurring injuries and patches of very lean form, but his penchant of showing up when it matters, in extremely emphatic fashion, hasn’t wavered with time. In a side that gets frequently noted for crumbling under pressure, faltering in the biggest moments, never being quite able to get over the line for true glory, Fakhar has churned out a reputation for himself that is the opposite. A ‘big match player’ is the sort of cliche that seems overwrought, but Fakhar has made it entirely his own. When it matters most, it is foolish to count him out. “The way my last 4 games had gone, a good performance was due,” he said during the post-match ceremony after scoring a match-winning century to lead Pakistan to triump in the One-day International tri-series final against Sri Lanka on Saturday. Fakhar Zaman celebrates his half century with Saad Baig alongside, during the tri-nation series final at the Gaddafi Stadium, Lahore, on Saturday, 31st October 2026.–AFP “Cricket is just like this, sometimes you are a good knick and sometimes you don’t score; even today I was struggling in the beginning.” “But I know that when it is my day, and the ball is coming onto my bat, I will score big.” And that he did – despite his lean returns in the first four matches Pakistan played in this tri-series, and despite the several scares he survived yesterday - wobbly shots, being dropped and given reprieves, Fakhar showed why giving him a life in a final has been, historically, a bad idea. Pakistan does not have a lot of time left with Fakhar. He is 36 years old, and will be 37 by the time next year’s World Cup in southern Africa is underway. It would probably be the most opportune moment for him to sign off on a memorable career, trying to give his team one shot at the ultimate glory in his favourite format. His century yesterday - 12th in ODIs, a record-breaking fourth in chases of more than 300 - is just one of those things Pakistan fans should learn to cherish when they get. But if yesterday showed anything, apart from reaffirming what Fakhar means to a Pakistan side, it was that Pakistan don’t have to be starved of time. In a match where Pakistan’s most trustworthy southpaw wielded his bat once again, it was one other that let him, and yet another that ensured it wouldn’t go to waste. Saad Baig had big shoes to fill coming into this ODI tri-nation series. With Mohammad Rizwan’s absence, Pakistan was not only missing a cog of the batting line-up that has been so crucial for so long, but also one of the finest pair of wicket-keeping gloves the country has sported. No one else has seemed good enough in comparison behind the stumps - either too undercooked, or too sloppy. Saad was Pakistan’s U-19 captain, and made his debut earlier in this tri-series. With a promising performance behind the stumps, and a string of starts with the bat that left one feeling unfulfilled but entirely assured of the pristine talent that shone through, the 19-year-old came out looking like he had a lot to prove. Ironically, he turns 20 today, following a knock yesterday that can only be described as a coming-of-age. If Fakhar was Pakistan’s anti-thesis to not showing up when it matters, Saad was the anti-thesis to a star performing batter never having enough support on the other end. “I have played domestic cricket with Saad, he is a very talented player,” Fakhar said, adding that Saad briskly scoring runs when he came to the crease yesterday allowed Fakhar to settle and take his time, and ultimately go big. “The credit goes to him for starting the way he did.” “Obviously there is pressure on you whenever you move to international cricket,” said Saad in a video reflection posted on PCB’s social media handles. “But the way you have to play through the pressure and back yourself, I was lacking that in the first two or three games, and was getting out in the 30s,” he added, saying that his plan for yesterday’s innings was to score while staying settled at the crease, and Fakhar’s “outstanding” innings made doing that all the more easier. He rotated strike and got into a good groove with Fakhar, rotating strike and picking out the Sri Lankan bowlers whenever the opportunity came to him. Perhaps the way he got out - an anticlimactic chip back to the bowler on a full Theekshana delivery - reflects where he stands in his career compared to the man across the other end, lacking just the final bit of grit and presence that can only come with time. And if these two left-handers set Pakistan on for victory, another one entirely made sure he finished it. Between overs 32.5 and 42.5, Pakistan did not score a single boundary. Fakhar and Salman Ali Agha had been bowled in quick succession. With Hasan Nawaz and Arafat new on the crease, and most of the toe-end of the innings left to bat through, their game plan seemed simple enough: don’t throw it away. The scoring during those overs came entirely from rotating strike, which might have felt grinding and underwhelming for an audience who had just witnessed a Fakhar Zaman special. Arafat Minhas plays a shot during the tri-nation series final at the Gaddafi Stadium, Lahore, on Saturday, 31st October 2026.–AFP It was a full Asitha Fernando delivery in the 45th over, drilled disdainfully down the ground, that would open the floodgates. In the bowler’s next over, Arafat hit possibly the cleanest, most sublime sequence of shots he has procured in his short career so far, bludgeoning two sixes and a four before holing out with Pakistan just two short of the win. “When I went in [to bat], I told Hasan that we have been through this situation before, and so we tried building a partnership,” he said. The two had carried out a deftly executed rescue job in their first tri-series fixture against England as well, ensuring Pakistan posted a total north of 300. “We backed each other and waited for bad balls to come to us.” “And I think through communicating with each other we had developed confidence in one another as well,” he said. Arafat was awarded player of the series as well - the second time he’s been awarded the title in as many ODI series he has participated in. “I have been saying from the beginning that I am an all-rounder,” he said in the ceremony. He was, after all, the leading architect with both bat and ball in Pakistan’s first win against England. “There is pressure, but the way you enjoy the pressure, stay calm during it, and execute your skills is important,” he said of the tricky place the team found itself in when he came in to bat with Hasan. Pakistan’s ODI assignments now all build up to the big shot at the big prize, the World Cup in South Africa next year. Young talents like Saad and Arafat is blooding in, and stalwarts like Fakhar hoping to find one final burst for the nation. What Pakistan can hope to take to South Africa is a team that sports both, the best of its recent past, and the most promising of its hopefully long future. And three left-handers on Saturday night in Lahore, showed exactly how to do it.

items.title: The Questions Adam Hamawy Won’t Answer
items.description: T he photograph, from April 1993 , shows a burly sheikh sitting on a couch wearing a gray kaftan, a white-and-crimson turban, and black sunglasses. His beard is thick and white. Reporters crowd into his Jersey City tenement apartment, waiting to hear him speak. Omar Abdel-Rahman—the man newspapers called the Blind Sheikh—by then had a reputation throughout the Muslim world as the religious leader of Egypt’s largest jihadist group. In 1981, his words inspired the assassins of President Anwar Sadat. His rhetoric could be unremitting, as in a speech in Brooklyn in early 1993: “We must be terrorists, and we must terrorize the enemies of Islam and frighten them and disturb them and shake the earth under their feet.” By spring of that year, law enforcement was investigating Abdel-Rahman’s possible involvement in at least two killings, including that of a prominent extremist rabbi. And that March, the FBI and foreign agencies had arrested several of Abdel-Rahman’s close followers, among them a man reported to be the sheikh’s part-time driver, on charges of helping carry out the February 1993 bombing of the World Trade Center, which killed six people but had aimed for far more. Adam Hamawy, who will almost certainly represent New Jersey’s Twelfth Congressional District come January, was at the press conference in the sheikh’s apartment the day the photograph was taken. He has said that he went there to translate something for Abdel-Rahman. Hamawy had met Abdel-Rahman two years earlier and became something of an acolyte, going to mosques across New Jersey to hear him speak, visiting the sheikh at home, and traveling with him to an Islamist conference in Detroit, where Abdel-Rahman and other speakers held forth on the necessity of violent jihad. In that photo, a bearded young man who resembles Hamawy kneels in front of reporters, his eyes trained on Abdel-Rahman. I asked Hamawy’s campaign multiple times whether that man is the candidate; the campaign did not reply. Najlah Feanny / Corbis / Getty Sheikh Omar Abdel-Rahman speaks at a press conference in Jersey City, New Jersey, in April 1993. Two months after that press conference, in June 1993, Abdel-Rahman would be arrested for plotting what would have been another catastrophic day of terrorism in New York City; the plan included blowing up two Hudson River tunnels and the United Nations, and assassinating the Egyptian leader Hosni Mubarak. Hamawy would testify as a defense witness at Abdel-Rahman’s trial in 1995, and Abdel-Rahman would be convicted and sentenced to life in prison. Today, Hamawy is a plastic surgeon in Princeton, New Jersey. He won his 12-candidate Democratic primary with 28 percent of the vote. Because his district is deep blue, he is expected to easily win his general election in November. Much about his story surely registers to voters as admirable. He was an infant when his family immigrated from Egypt to Old Bridge, a town of about 50,000 at the time, located 35 miles south of New York City. He worked through college and medical school, went to Ground Zero to care for rescue workers, and served in Iraq as a U.S. Army combat surgeon. He restored bodies broken by war—including that of Tammy Duckworth, now a U.S. senator, who lost her legs when a rocket-propelled grenade hit her helicopter. She has credited Hamawy with saving her life. Hamawy already has found a place on the Democratic Party’s left wing. Although he is an observant Muslim—on primary night, he led supporters in chants of “Allahu Akbar!” ( God is greater )—he is, unlike some fellow believers, pro-choice and an advocate for LGBTQ rights. He is passionate in his support for Medicare for All and in his insistence that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza. Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have endorsed him. Hamawy himself has endorsed and appeared with the Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, and campaigned with the far-left streamer Hasan Piker, who once said that “America deserved 9/11.” Hamawy has also declined to commit to backing House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, saying that the Democratic congressional leadership is “failing to meet the moment.” Throughout his campaign, Hamawy has not fully accounted for why, as a young man, he kept company with Abdel-Rahman and others in his circle. Perhaps Hamawy was merely young, curious, and hapless and did not fully buy into the sheikh’s ideas. Or perhaps he harbored beliefs that he has since renounced. Hamawy himself has provided little explanation. When asked during the primary about Abdel-Rahman, who died in 2017, and his terrorism conspiracy, Hamawy told NBC , “I absolutely regret, and I condemn, what happened.” At the same time, he dismissed reporting about his relationship with the sheikh, attributing it to “right-wing media” and adding, “It’s racist. It’s really anti-Muslim.” Former Attorney General Michael Mukasey, who presided over Abdel-Rahman’s terror trial as a federal judge, has called the sheikh “one of the world’s leading theologians of terrorism.” And Abdel-Rahman’s influence continued after his conviction: While serving out a life sentence in prison, the sheikh issued the fatwa that Osama bin Laden would use to justify the September 11 attacks. In August, I spoke with Hamawy by phone for about an hour, and when he talked about health care or being a son of immigrants, he was expansive and friendly. But when I asked about the years when he drew close to Abdel-Rahman, he began to bob and weave—as he had in his testimony during the sheikh’s 1995 trial—and sometimes contradicted himself, even as he said that there was nothing of interest to be discovered. “This characterization as a ‘relationship,’ I think, really misrepresents things,” he told me. He has repeatedly referred to the sheikh—who was in his 50s when Hamawy met him—as a “blind old man.” Hamawy noted his U.S. military service and his promotion to lieutenant colonel: “Clearly I was trusted by our government to be able to perform these services.” At one point, when I was pushing for more details, he bristled: “Clearly, clearly you have nothing else to talk about.” His spokesperson eventually ended the interview, and has not responded to multiple emails with additional questions. Hannah Beier / The New York Times / Redux Adam Hamawy and Hasan Piker at a campaign event in Trenton, New Jersey, in May H amawy described Abdel-Rahman in the early 1990s as akin to a religious celebrity. “This was a person who was really everywhere in New York and New Jersey,” he told me, at a time when there were “not many leaders” in the Muslim community. “He was someone who led prayers and was known for his recitation of the Quran.” Abdel-Rahman was in fact known for far more. The jihadist group in Egypt for which he acted as the religious authority , Gama’a al-Islamiyya, employed deadly violence in an effort to establish extremist Islamic rule in Egypt. Abdel-Rahman had declared in sermons that Sadat, the Egyptian president, was an infidel. He was jailed after Sadat’s death, but judges acquitted him on charges that he had sanctioned it; they ruled that although he had told his followers they had a duty to kill wayward Muslim leaders such as Sadat, there was not enough evidence to prove that Abdel-Rahman had directed the assassination. In 1990, a follower of Abdel-Rahman’s, El Sayyid Nosair, assassinated the radical right-wing rabbi Meir Kahane, who had twice been convicted on terrorism-related charges, in New York City. Hamawy has said that he first heard the sheikh give a talk in 1991 in Matawan, New Jersey, and in his telling, their meeting afterward was incidental. “I met him,” Hamawy told me, not offering much more detail, “like so many others.” This understates the nature of their eventual relationship, by Hamawy’s own previous account. In 1995, when the legal team defending Abdel-Rahman in his federal terrorism trial called Hamawy to testify , he made a point of greeting the sheikh, and mentioned phone calls, travel, and visits with Abdel-Rahman. “I have seen him in, you know, speak at different mosques all over New Jersey,” Hamawy said, according to the trial transcript. “I have seen him in his home.” He mentioned seeing the sheikh at a school “several times.” In November 1991, Abdel-Rahman was invited to speak at an Islamic conference in Detroit, and Hamawy joined him on the 13-hour drive there in a minivan, along with five other men. (Some of the details of Hamawy’s backstory were first reported by The Washington Free Beacon and Jewish Insider .) Hamawy described his decision to travel to Detroit as a sort of lark. “I was a last-minute carpool,” he said in our interview. “I’m a college student.” (He had graduated from Rutgers earlier that year.) “It’s a free ride to go somewhere. It wasn’t like I was following him.” Yet Hamawy testified during the trial that in Detroit, some of the men from the van shared a hotel suite; Hamawy was in the same room as Abdel-Rahman. Hamawy attended the conference too, and listened to the sheikh’s speech about jihad and the speeches of other hard-line Islamists. Lorenzo Vidino, who studies Islamic extremism and directs the Program on Extremism at George Washington University, told me that it is highly unlikely that Abdel-Rahman and members of his inner circle would throw open a door to a random newcomer. “You have in Abdel-Rahman one of the two or three godfathers of radical jihad in the world,” Vidino said. “There’s no chance for an outsider to spend meaningful time in a minivan with the Blind Sheikh.” Earlier this year, Mukasey, the judge in the trial, wrote in The Wall Street Journal, “Mr. Hamawy was more than a casual traveling companion of Abdel Rahman.” [ From the November 2012 issue: My conversion will not be televised ] The conference the men attended was titled “Towards a Global Islamic Economy,” and under questioning by Abdel-Rahman’s lawyer during the trial, Hamawy said that the event was focused on the economy. He told the defense lawyer that he had never heard Abdel-Rahman talk about jihad in America. Nor, Hamawy said in reply to a question from the prosecutor, had he heard Abdel-Rahman talk about robbing banks or attacking military bases. Then one of the prosecutors, Patrick Fitzgerald, commenced his cross-examination of Hamawy. Do you recall, he asked, if Abdel-Rahman talked about the Egyptian leader Mubarak in Detroit? “Not really,” Hamawy replied. Fitzgerald handed Hamawy a transcript of the sheikh’s speech from the conference and gave him a moment to read it. Then he rephrased his question more pointedly: Do you recall Abdel-Rahman that weekend talking about Mubarak as “the backstabber who became the loyal dog to America?” Hamawy, his memory apparently refreshed, responded: “Yes.” Fitzgerald asked Hamawy if Abdel-Rahman had talked in his speech about jihad and the importance of conquering the land of the infidels. Hamawy quibbled about wording and definitions but conceded that Abdel-Rahman’s speech centered on “a struggle in the sake of God, yes. It was a jihad.” (Fitzgerald quoted from speeches of Abdel-Rahman’s several times in the trial, making clear what the sheikh meant by that word, jihad . For example: “If God, glory be to him, says do jihad, it means do jihad with the sword, with the cannon, with the grenades, and with a missile.”) Among the other speakers at the Detroit conference was Hassan al-Turabi, the leader of a repressive, violent Islamist movement in Sudan and a friend of Abdel-Rahman’s. As the trial went on, the prosecutor burrowed in, asking if the sheikh had ever described America and Israel as enemies of Islam. Yes, Hamawy replied. Fitzgerald then asked if Hamawy had ever heard Abdel-Rahman say that Muslims have an obligation to carry out jihad against enemies of Islam. “Of course,” Hamawy replied. “That’s what he always talked about. He talked about jihad, you know.” The successful prosecution of Abdel-Rahman and nine others hinged largely on the testimony of Emad Salem , an undercover informant for the U.S. government. Salem had infiltrated Abdel-Rahman’s circle, pretending to be a disaffected Egyptian special-forces soldier turned jihadist, and was one of the band who traveled in the van to Detroit. One day during that trip, Salem testified, Abdel-Rahman took the group, Hamawy included, back to the hotel suite. They sat on the floor, and Abdel-Rahman grilled Salem on his military knowledge: Do you know dynamite? Yes, Salem said. Did he know how to blow dynamite up? Again, Salem replied yes. Then Abdel-Rahman inquired about Salem’s skill as a shooter. “He ask [ sic ] me to turn my rifle to President Mubarak’s chest,” Salem testified. Hamawy, in his testimony, denied ever witnessing such a conversation, though he noted that Salem frequently talked in front of the sheikh about his abilities with bombs. He said that he and the rest of Abdel-Rahman’s circle suspected that Salem might be working for Egyptian intelligence and trying to entrap the sheikh. Salem was a complicated figure who had lied under oath in the past. The lead federal prosecutor in the trial, Andrew McCarthy, later referred to him as “the strangest, wiliest, most impossible, most infuriating pain in the ass I ever will know.” But McCarthy also called him “breathtakingly effective.” Salem managed to tape-record countless hours of his conversations with suspects (though he was not able to record the conversation in which he said the sheikh told him to turn his gun on Mubarak). Jurors judged Salem credible enough to convict 10 men on 48 of 50 charges. A federal appeals-court panel unanimously affirmed the verdicts. There was, according to Salem, more talk of rifle shooting on the drive from Detroit back to New Jersey. One of Abdel-Rahman’s followers asked Salem if he could train him and other followers in rifle target practice. In code, the men called it “deer hunting.” This follower told Salem that he and other followers hadn’t gotten a chance to practice with rifles since Nosair, who had organized past trainings, had been arrested. Can we, the follower asked, go deer hunting with you? Salem agreed: “I said, ‘Sure, why not, we will do that.’” Hamawy, who was in the van at that time, was not asked during the trial about that conversation, nor did he speak of it on his own. Hamawy remained on friendly terms with the sheikh after the Detroit conference. In the summer of 1992, before Hamawy entered medical school, he and two friends took a pilgrimage to Mecca and visited Egypt and London; Hamawy also stopped in Jerusalem. When asked during the trial who had recommended his travel agent, Hamawy answered: “Sheikh Omar.” A friend of the sheikh, he said, accompanied the young men on their flight to London. There, Hamawy testified, they relied on yet another friend of the sheikh, a man who worked in an Islamic bookstore, who found them a youth hostel. At least two of the men Hamawy and his friends met on that trip, including the bookstore worker, were suspected members of Gama’a al-Islamiyya , prosecutors said. When Hamawy and his friends returned to London on their way home, Hamawy testified, he made sure to call the bookstore worker and thank him for his hospitality. Hamawy was asked during the trial if he knew what Gama’a al-Islamiyya was and said that he had heard of it; asked if he knew any members of the organization, he said, “I assume that Sheikh Omar was, yes.” Once Hamawy entered medical school, he saw less of Abdel-Rahman. The sheikh was very much in the news in 1993 as followers of his were being investigated for their role in the World Trade Center bombing. In April of that year, Hamawy called Abdel-Rahman. “I hadn’t been able to see Sheikh Omar that much,” he testified in the federal trial. “I had called him earlier that week and told him: ‘It is my spring break now. If you need anything, you can just give me a call.’” As it happened, the sheikh called and asked Hamawy to translate a document for him as he was getting ready to hold the press conference in his Jersey City apartment. The generous explanation for Hamawy’s affiliation with Abdel-Rahman is youthful fascination. It’s not unusual for young people to be captivated by radical leaders, only to wise up and turn away as the years pass. The American left offers many such examples of this, from those attracted by Soviet Communism in the 1930s to those who embraced the violence of the Weathermen and the Black Panthers. Young socialist Iranians embraced Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini in 1979, only for many thousands to end up before his firing squads in years to come. In our interview, I asked Hamawy if there was something about Abdel-Rahman that spoke to him as a young man. Was he merely intrigued, or something like a true believer? He pushed back on my question. “It wasn’t a personal relationship,” he said. “This is where reality and fiction is beginning to kind of diverge.” I n the course of his medical career, Hamawy has worked on missions of mercy in countries including Haiti, Sudan, Lebanon, and Syria; in 2024 and 2025, he spent several weeks at hospitals in Gaza. The details of two such missions raise additional questions. By 1994, Yugoslavia had dissolved, and three of its republics—Bosnia, Croatia, and Serbia—had descended into brutal ethnic and religious wars. About half of Bosnia’s roughly 4 million citizens were Muslim, and Bosnian Serb and Serbian military units carried out massacres and mass rapes against them. The suffering of Bosnia’s Muslims was a subject that consumed many millions of Muslims, and others, around the globe. Several witnesses in Abdel-Rahman’s federal trial testified that the sheikh and his followers spoke often of Bosnia and the duty of Muslims to fight jihad there. No evidence suggests that Abdel-Rahman encouraged Hamawy to go to Bosnia. But as a medical student, he was among those who wanted to help. In the summer of 1994, Hamawy told me, he reached out to the Bosnian Mission to the United Nations, and asked about volunteering. In a 1996 interview with The New Jersey Star-Ledger , he said that the mission had recommended that he reach out to Benevolence International, a charity with offices in several countries, including the United States and Bosnia. Hamawy spent his first week in Sarajevo and the next four in Zenica, a hill city about an hour away. As he described it to me, he stayed with two local doctors and spent his days going to the charity’s warehouse and delivering medical supplies to local clinics. Zenica was a contested and violent place at that time. Jihadists who had fought against the Soviets in Afghanistan and the Russians in Chechnya were pouring into Bosnia. Zenica became the headquarters of the notorious brigade known as Odred El Mudžahid, or “The Jihadist Unit,” composed of foreign fighters from across the Middle East and Chechnya. A human-rights criminal tribunal later found that from 1993 to March 1994, the brigade had engaged in torture, looting, and massacres of Christian Croats and Serbs, soldiers and civilians alike, some of whom were beheaded ; in January 1994, gunmen from the brigade had executed a British aid worker outside of Zenica. Much later, some commanders affiliated with the brigade were convicted of war crimes. Benevolence International was an important player in that jihadist ecosystem. In the years after its incorporation in 1992, the charity provided medical assistance to impoverished Bosnian refugees. But during those same years, its guiding force was Osama bin Laden: According to the 9/11 Commission Report , Benevolence International’s office in Sarajevo was one of bin Laden’s “impressive array” of offices providing financial and technical support for terrorism. After 9/11, the U.S. and Bosnia and Herzegovina investigated the group and raided several of its offices. They found many compelling links to al-Qaeda, including a photograph taken in Afghanistan in the late 1980s showing the Benevolence International director Enaam Arnaout and bin Laden holding rifles and a shoulder-fired rocket. They also discovered a handwritten letter in which bin Laden authorized Arnaout to sign on his behalf, and documents establishing that Arnaout had worked with members of al-Qaeda to purchase rockets, mortars, rifles, and bombs to distribute to fighter camps, including those of al-Qaeda. In 2002, Arnaout was indicted on charges of racketeering, money laundering, and concealing his terrorism ties, and the Treasury Department designated Benevolence a “financier of terror.” Arnaout pleaded guilty to illegally siphoning off charitable contributions to buy uniforms and other supplies for fighters in Bosnia and Chechnya, though as part of the plea agreement, prosecutors dropped the terrorism-related charges against him. (In 2005, a lawyer who had represented Benevolence International, Matthew J. Piers, wrote a defense of the organization in which he argued that the U.S. government’s investigation had caused its “malevolent destruction.”) Hamawy told me that he knew nothing at the time about the group’s ties to al-Qaeda or its support for jihadist fighters. He simply believed that he was working with staff at what he told me was a UN-endorsed charity to deliver supplies to clinics overwhelmed with the sick and dying. (The UN did not keep a list of certified charities in Bosnia.) “I had no sense or even suspicion anything like that was happening,” he said. “To kind of imply that between my microbiology rotation and my psychiatry rotation, I was in the mountains acting as, like, you know, some nefarious player is, again, kind of ludicrous.” When I spoke with Jeffrey Parsons, who led FBI anti-terror investigations for two decades and now works for the George Washington University Program on Extremism, he was inclined to believe Hamawy’s claim to ignorance about the specifics of the charity’s subterfuge. Al-Qaeda-linked charities often played a double game, and those on the medical side might have known little about the money and aid sluiced off for jihadists. Still, as with his ties to Abdel-Rahman, Hamawy’s apparent lack of curiosity is itself curious. “It is an interesting life choice,” Parsons told me. “He definitely went there willingly, and he was in a city and a charity that would become a core for big shots in al-Qaeda.” [ From the September 2026 issue: What happened to al-Qaeda? ] Decades later, in 2024 and 2025, Hamawy journeyed to Gaza for another medical mission as Israeli bombs fell around him. He worked at the European Hospital in 2024 and Nasser Hospital in 2025, and said that he was seared by the experience. The war there was more horrifying than any he had seen before, particularly for children, he told me. He has been adamant in interviews that Hamas had no presence in or underneath these hospitals. He told me that as a surgeon he could walk anywhere, that he had a trained eye, and that he saw no signs of militants or weapons. In 2024, he told Jacobin magazine that he had not seen a single weapon at the European Hospital: “Not one rifle. Not one pistol. Not one grenade launcher. This was a completely benign civilian hospital with no tunnels underneath it.” ABC News asked him about Israeli and U.S. intelligence that Hamas gunmen had access to Nasser Hospital. “Their intelligence is just wrong,” Hamawy said. “In terms of operations and people, actually fighters that are actively in, that has not been observed by anyone that’s been in these hospitals over the last two years.” Yet in the spring of 2025, the Israelis ordered staff and patients at the European Hospital to leave and bombed directly outside. Afterward, Israel said that its forces had found the body of Mohammed Sinwar, then the military leader of Hamas, in a tunnel that ran beneath the hospital emergency room. (His brother, Yahya Sinwar, had directed the October 7, 2023, invasion of southern Israel.) In January 2026, Doctors Without Borders suspended “non-critical” medical operations at Nasser Hospital, stating: “Our teams have reported the presence of armed men, some of them masked; intimidation; arbitrary arrests of patients; and a recent situation involving the suspected movement of weapons.” Israel and the U.S., as well as The New York Times , have found evidence of Hamas’s presence at another hospital in Gaza, al-Shifa. Last year, I spoke with medical personnel who had worked there and at other Gaza hospitals. “You knew Hamas was there; I went to meetings where this was made very clear,” one Doctors Without Borders staffer told me . “Doors were hidden. There were units you did not get into, that had armed guards at the door.” I asked Hamawy about Sinwar’s death underneath the European Hospital. Hamas confirmed more than a year ago that the Israelis had killed Sinwar, and has not disputed that he died in that tunnel. The Israeli military also took a group of foreign reporters, including from The New York Times and NBC News , through the tunnel under the hospital to the bloodstained room where Israeli forces said Sinwar had died. “I don’t believe anything until we have third-party observers on the ground,” Hamawy told me. “To take the word of the Israelis and not take the word of the Palestinians seems kind of, like, illogical.” The Israelis, he said, “show you pictures that, to my experienced eye, look at it and say, ‘Hey, something doesn’t look right about this picture.’” The problem for Hamawy is that, in the past, his intuitions have proven quite fallible. At one point in our interview , Hamawy said that my line of questioning about the sheikh was “trying to characterize me, like everyone else is characterizing me, as: ‘Oh my God, this man is a Muslim man who came in contact with someone who, again, you know, ended up, like, serving for crimes, for years that I have condemned.’” I could find no public evidence that Hamawy had denounced Abdel-Rahman prior to his candidacy and the media’s unearthing of that history. More to the point, asking about that history is fair game. He owes a fuller explanation to his would-be constituents. Perhaps voters simply are no longer paying attention to his campaign. Hamawy’s Republican opponent, Gregg Mele , has no money and even less mojo; he is a near-perpetual candidate in New Jersey who has yet to come close to winning a seat. Most reporters have stopped covering the race, other than to track Hamawy’s encounters with other Democratic politicians on the left. In August, he attended the annual Panamerican Congress, a meeting of left-wing leaders in the Americas, held this year in Uruguay. And he and another likely U.S. representative, Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York, served as keynote speakers at the annual gala of the Council on American-Islamic Relations in Washington, D.C. Micah Rasmussen, director of the Rebovich Institute for New Jersey Politics, points out that New Jersey sits between two big media markets, New York City and Philadelphia, and remains an afterthought in both. “Political junkies to the side, a lot of people don’t know what’s going on,” Rasmussen told me about Hamawy’s race. “But you can count me as a person who thinks that there are really important questions left about his background.” If we are to assume that Hamawy’s political coming of age included a turn away from men such as Abdel-Rahman, the puzzle is why he does not talk candidly about that change of heart, rather than continuing to insist that to ask such questions is hateful.
